name: Marco Polo on Khubilai's paper money
text: The Emperor’s Mint then is in this same City of Cambaluc, and the way it is wrought is such that you might say he hath the Secret of Alchemy in perfection, and you would be right! ... And the Kaan causes every year to be made such a vast quantity of this money, which costs him nothing, that it must equal in amount all the treasure in the world. ... With these pieces of paper, made as I have described, he causes all payments on his own account to be made; and he makes them to pass current universally over all his kingdoms and provinces and territories, and whithersoever his power and sovereignty extends. And nobody, however important he may think himself, dares to refuse them on pain of death.
author: person:marco_polo
work: The Travels, Book II, ch. 24 (tr. Yule, rev. Cordier)
witness: Dictated in a Genoese prison in 1298 to the romance writer Rustichello, and surviving in many divergent manuscripts. Polo had real access to the Yuan court, but he writes for a European audience amazed by the exotic and exaggerates freely; the claim that the money 'costs him nothing' is the outsider's view of a system that, as von Glahn shows, depended on convertibility and collapsed by the 1350s when that broke.

name: Marco Polo on Hangzhou, the former Song capital
text: the city is beyond dispute the finest and the noblest in the world. ... First and foremost, then, the document stated the city of Kinsay to be so great that it hath an hundred miles of compass. And there are in it twelve thousand bridges of stone, for the most part so lofty that a great fleet could pass beneath them. ... The document aforesaid also stated that the number and wealth of the merchants, and the amount of goods that passed through their hands, was so enormous that no man could form a just estimate thereof.
author: person:marco_polo
work: The Travels, Book II, ch. 76 (tr. Yule, rev. Cordier)
witness: Polo says he is repeating a document the Song queen sent to the Mongol general Bayan to persuade him to spare the city, so the numbers (a hundred-mile circuit, 12,000 bridges) are a surrendering court's boast passed through a Venetian's memory. The impression of a vast commercial city is confirmed by Chinese sources; the figures are not.

name: Marco Polo on Mongol horses and armies
text: They are also more capable of hardships than other nations; for many a time, if need be, they will go for a month without any supply of food, living only on the milk of their mares and on such game as their bows may win them. Their horses also will subsist entirely on the grass of the plains, so that there is no need to carry store of barley or straw or oats; ... Of all troops in the world these are they which endure the greatest hardship and fatigue, and which cost the least; and they are the best of all for making wide conquests of country.
author: person:marco_polo
work: The Travels, Book I, ch. 54 (tr. Yule, rev. Cordier)
witness: Written two generations after the conquests by a Venetian in Mongol service, who admired his masters. The point about horses living on grass alone is exactly what makes pasture, and therefore rainfall, a military resource; Polo had no idea of the 1211-25 pluvial, which is why his testimony is useful rather than tendentious here.

name: Adam Smith: China 'long stationary'
text: China has been long one of the richest, that is, one of the most fertile, best cultivated, most industrious, and most populous, countries in the world. It seems, however, to have been long stationary. Marco Polo, who visited it more than five hundred years ago, describes its cultivation, industry, and populousness, almost in the same terms in which they are described by travellers in the present times. It had, perhaps, even long before his time, acquired that full complement of riches which the nature of its laws and institutions permits it to acquire. The accounts of all travellers, inconsistent in many other respects, agree in the low wages of labour, and in the difficulty which a labourer finds in bringing up a family in China.
author: person:adam_smith
work: The Wealth of Nations, Book I, ch. 8
witness: Smith never went to China; he relied on Marco Polo and Jesuit and travellers' reports, mostly about the coast and Canton. His 'stationary' China is a theoretical foil for his argument about growing and declining wages, yet his claim of low wages broadly matches what Allen and colleagues find in 18th-century wage data.

name: Adam Smith: China's riches limited by 'laws and institutions'
text: China seems to have been long stationary, and had, probably, long ago acquired that full complement of riches which is consistent with the nature of its laws and institutions. But this complement may be much inferior to what, with other laws and institutions, the nature of its soil, climate, and situation, might admit of. A country which neglects or despises foreign commerce, and which admits the vessel of foreign nations into one or two of its ports only, cannot transact the same quantity of business which it might do with different laws and institutions.
author: person:adam_smith
work: The Wealth of Nations, Book I, ch. 9
witness: Written while the Canton system (from 1757) confined European trade to one port, which Smith reads as the whole of Chinese commercial policy. It is the founding text of the institutional explanation of the divergence; note that China's vast internal trade, which impressed Pomeranz and Wong, is invisible to him.

name: Malthus on China's population and famines
text: China seems to answer to this description. If the accounts we have of it are to be trusted, the lower classes of people are in the habit of living almost upon the smallest possible quantity of food and are glad to get any putrid offals that European labourers would rather starve than eat. The law in China which permits parents to expose their children has tended principally thus to force the population. A nation in this state must necessarily be subject to famines.
author: person:thomas_robert_malthus
work: An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), ch. 7
witness: Malthus says himself 'if the accounts we have of it are to be trusted': like Smith he relied on Jesuit and travellers' reports. Lee and Wang argue the picture is a myth, since Chinese families controlled births and Qing granaries damped famine; Elvin's trap is a more sophisticated descendant of this passage.

name: Bai Juyi: the old man who broke his own arm
text: Of three men in each house,--one man was taken. And those to whom the lot fell, where were they taken to? Five months’ journey, a thousand miles--away to Yün-nan. ... Everyone says that in expeditions against the Min tribes Of a million men who are sent out, not one returns. ... I secretly took a huge stone and dashed it against my arm. ... That the Prime Minister of T’ien-Pao, Yang Kuo-chung ... Desiring to win imperial favour, started a frontier war?
author: person:bai_juyi
work: 'The Old Man with the Broken Arm' (tr. Arthur Waley)
witness: Bai Juyi wrote this 'new music-bureau' poem around 809, half a century after the Yunnan campaigns of 751-754, as deliberate political satire against frontier adventurism. The old man is a literary device; the 'million men' is hyperbole. Its value is as evidence of how the Tianbao wars were remembered at court after An Lushan.

name: Du Fu: the recruiting sergeant
text: A grim recruiting sergeant, of the kind That seize their prey by night. ... Once I had three sons -- Three in the Emperor's camp. ... My two dead boys! for ever and for aye Death holds them.
author: person:du_fu
work: 'The Officer at Shihao' (free version by L. Cranmer-Byng as 'The Recruiting Sergeant')
witness: Du Fu wrote the poem in 759 after the Tang defeat at Xiangzhou, when press-gangs swept Henan for men. Cranmer-Byng's 1909 rendering is a loose Edwardian verse paraphrase, not a translation, so use it for the scene, not the wording. It shows why households fled the registers: every registered man was a conscript.

name: Arthur Waley's 1918 gloss: 'thirty million men'
text: In 755 the Emperor’s Turkic favourite, An Lu-shan, revolted against his master. A civil war followed, in which China lost thirty million men. The dynasty was permanently enfeebled and the Empire greatly curtailed by foreign incursions.
author: person:arthur_waley
work: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems, introduction
witness: Not a Tang source: a great translator's 1918 introduction, here as a witness to how the registration collapse was read as a death toll. Waley takes the census fall literally; Durand and later demographers show most of the 'lost' millions slipped off the registers. The source of a still-viral myth.

name: Mendoza on China, from books brought to Manila
text: This mightie kingdome, which we commonly call China, without knowing any cause or foundation wherefore we should so cal it, those countries neere ioyning vnto the same, do call it Sangley: and they in their naturall toonge do cal it Taybiner,[26] the which is to be vnderstood, nothing but a kingdome: and is the most biggest and populous that is mentioned in all the world, ... All the which is taken out of the bookes and hystories of the said Chinos, whereas they do make mention of the mightinesse thereof, and of the 15 prouinces that are comprehended in the same: the which bookes and hystories were brought vnto the citie of Manilla, printed and set forth in China, and were translated into the Spanish toong, by interpreters of the saide nations.
author: person:juan_gonzalez_de_mendoza
work: History of the Great and Mighty Kingdom of China (1585), tr. Robert Parke (1588)
witness: An Augustinian friar who never reached China compiled this bestseller from missionary reports and Chinese books bought in Manila, the new market where American silver met Chinese junks after 1571. Its figures come from Ming registers via translators; its awe reflects how Europeans saw Ming wealth at the height of the silver trade.

sources.cite: González de Mendoza, tr. Parke, ed. Staunton (1853)

name: A Taiping sympathiser on the ruined delta
text: I found a considerable tract of land perfectly desolated, not a dwelling nor habitation of any sort standing, and the fields untended, with the rice or paddy growing wild. It appeared this part had been severely contested by the Ti-ping and Imperialist troops, and between them it had become a solitude.
author: person:augustus_lindley
work: Ti-Ping Tien-Kwoh: The History of the Ti-Ping Revolution, vol. 1
witness: Lindley, a British adventurer who served the Taiping, wrote to defend them and attack British intervention, so he blames devastation on both sides or on the Imperialists. His eyewitness descriptions of empty, overgrown country near the silk districts are consistent with Meyer-Fong's sources.

name: Lindley protests British intervention against the Taiping
text: In writing this work I have been prompted by feelings of sympathy for a worthy, oppressed, and cruelly-wronged people; as well as by a desire to protest against the evil foreign policy which England, during the last few years, has pursued towards _weak_ Powers, especially in Asia.
author: person:augustus_lindley
work: Ti-Ping Tien-Kwoh: The History of the Ti-Ping Revolution, preface
witness: A partisan's preface, written in London after the Taiping fell. Its value is as evidence that the British switch from neutrality to intervention, central to Platt's argument, was controversial in Britain at the time.

name: Ernest Satow on the shogun's 'double game'
text: I overheard a man in the market say "the _Bakufu_ is playing a double game." ... Then I gave them our view of the case, which was that the Tycoon, finding himself in a tight place between the _daimiôs_ and the foreigners, had to give assurances to both which were inconsistent with each other,
author: person:ernest_satow
witness: Satow, a British interpreter, wrote this memoir decades later from his diaries; he became openly sympathetic to Choshu and Satsuma, the eventual winners. The scene at Shimonoseki in 1864 nonetheless captures the shogunate's impossible position between the treaty powers and the anti-foreign domains.

name: The Imperial Rescript on Education
text: Ye, Our subjects, be filial to your parents, affectionate to your brothers and sisters; as husbands and wives be harmonious, as friends true; bear yourselves in modesty and moderation; extend your benevolence to all; pursue learning and cultivate arts, and thereby develop intellectual faculties and perfect moral powers; furthermore advance public good and promote common interests; always respect the Constitution and observe the laws; should emergency arise, offer yourselves courageously to the State
author: person:emperor_meiji
work: Imperial Rescript on Education (official English translation)
witness: A state text read aloud at every school ceremony until 1945: it shows the Meiji state fusing Confucian family ethics with service to the nation and the throne. It is prescription, not description of how Japanese actually behaved, and the official English version softens the original's sacral language.
author_name: Emperor Meiji (drafted by Inoue Kowashi and Motoda Nagazane)
